title: Weak-coupling tensor cross interpolation impurity solver for nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory
authors: Shuta Matsuura, Hiroshi Shinaoka, Philipp Werner, Naoto Tsuji
abstract: Simulating nonequilibrium quantum many-body systems remains a major challenge due to the exponential growth of the computational complexity with real time. Here we implement a nonequilibrium impurity solver based on the weak-coupling expansion and the tensor cross interpolation (TCI), and apply it to nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT). The method approximates the integrands of the high-dimensional integrals arising in the weak-coupling expansion in a tensor-train form, enabling efficient evaluations without stochastic sampling and thereby mitigating the sign problem affecting continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo (CT-QMC) methods. Benchmark calculations for an exactly solvable nonequilibrium impurity model agree well with the exact results and reveal a low-rank structure of the integrands. When applied to interaction-quench problems in the half-filled Hubbard model, the method reproduces fast thermalization at a critical interaction strength with accuracy comparable to CT-QMC. Away from half filling, where the sign problem becomes even more severe, the present approach remains well controlled, revealing a crossover instead of a sharply defined fast thermalization point in the 3/4-filled case. The solver can also be applied to steady-state DMFT problems, yielding accurate spectral functions in the metallic regime without analytic continuation.
summary: This paper introduces a novel impurity solver for nonequilibrium Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) by combining a weak-coupling expansion with Tensor Cross Interpolation (TCI). This technique efficiently handles high-dimensional integrals on the Keldysh contour, circumventing the sign problem that plagues standard Monte Carlo methods. It allows accurate simulation of quantum quenches in correlated models like the Hubbard model.
main_problem: Simulating nonequilibrium quantum many-body systems, which suffer from exponential computational complexity with real time.
main_result: The developed TCI solver successfully implements an impurity solver for nonequilibrium DMFT, accurately reproducing thermalization dynamics and remaining controlled away from the sign problem region.
method: It combines a weak-coupling expansion with the Tensor Cross Interpolation (TCI) algorithm to efficiently evaluate high-dimensional integrals arising in the Keldysh formalism without stochastic sampling.
model_or_system: The method is applied to nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated electron systems, specifically using the mass-imbalanced Hubbard model on a lattice structure within the framework of Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT).
key_observables: Nonequilibrium Green's functions ($G_\sigma(z, z')$), spectral functions, and thermalization behavior.
important_parameters: Interaction strength ($U$), filling fraction ($\delta\mu$), maximum simulation time ($t_{max}$), and the weak-coupling expansion order ($n_{max}$).
main_assumptions: The method relies on approximating high-dimensional integrals using a tensor-train decomposition (TCI) and assumes sufficient smoothness for extrapolation across the Keldysh contour.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the L-shaped Kadanoff–Baym contour, convergence of TCI results with increasing order ($n_{max}$), and phase diagrams showing solver performance across different coupling regimes.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the complex Green's function formalism on the Keldysh contour to implementing the weak-coupling expansion. It details the use of TCI for integral evaluation, applies this to both transient dynamics (quenches) and steady states, and concludes with benchmarking against known limits.
why_interesting: The development of a robust, non-stochastic solver for nonequilibrium DMFT is crucial for studying open quantum systems driven far from equilibrium, bridging the gap between weak-coupling perturbation theory and complex time evolution simulations.
